Coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) exhibit a characteristic semelparous life history, where individuals typically spawn once before death. During alevin development within the gravel redd, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until the point of first exogenous feeding. Freshly emerged alevins have a wet weight at birth of only approximately 0.3137 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.3137 grams], a value that reflects the initial endowment carried through yolk absorption. The timing of this emergence is strongly temperature-dependent; at a mean incubation temperature of 4.6 °C [T = 4.6 °C], the age at birth from egg fertilisation is approximately 145.5 days [ab = approximately 145.5 days], indicating a relatively prolonged embryonic period under these cool conditions typical of northern spawning grounds. This extended incubation contrasts with the patterns observed in more southerly populations where warmer water temperatures can accelerate developmental rates substantially.

Research on the species’ maximum attainable size has revealed considerable variation across its geographic range. Although historical records from some systems suggest a ultimate total length of 108 cm [Li = 108 cm], contemporary fisheries data from coastal watersheds often indicate that individuals rarely exceed 80 cm in fork length. This asymptotic size is closely linked to the reproductive strategy. During their ocean residency, which spans several years, these fish accumulate substantial body mass to support the energetically demanding freshwater migration and spawning event. The ultimate wet weight achieved by a mature adult before senescence is approximately 15,200 grams [Wwi = approximately 15,200 grams], a value that correlates with the large body sizes recorded in certain Alaskan stocks. Such an investment in somatic growth prior to the terminal spawning run is a defining feature of the species' life history template.

Puberty, marking the onset of reproductive maturation, occurs after a defined period of growth in the marine environment. The time since birth at puberty for Coho salmon reared under optimal thermal conditions of 5 °C [T = 5 °C] has been estimated at 1,095 days [tp = 1,095 days], which is equivalent to approximately three years of ocean feeding. Accompanying this developmental milestone is a substantial increase in body dimensions; the total length at puberty is recorded at approximately 77 cm [Lp = approximately 77 cm], reflecting the scale of growth achieved during the sub-adult phase. The associated wet weight at puberty is approximately 10,800 grams [Wwp = approximately 10,800 grams], an intermediate mass that denotes the transition from the immature, feeding stage to a state of reproductive competence. This weight is consistent with the condition factor observed in returning adults in many Pacific Northwest rivers.

For a semelparous species like Coho salmon, the final reproductive output is a singular, life-ending event. Spawning females deposit all their eggs in a single spawning event, and there is no subsequent reproduction. The lifetime fecundity, measured as eggs at the end of life, has been estimated at 6,906 eggs  for individuals reared under a constant water temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]. This substantial number represents a considerable investment of the maternal energy reserves that were accumulated over the preceding years of marine feeding. The maximum lifespan, from egg deposition to post-spawning mortality, under these same thermal conditions of 5 °C [T = 5 °C] is approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days], which equates to roughly five years. This complete lifespan encompasses the freshwater incubation, riverine migration, and the extended oceanic feeding phase before the final spawning run.

From a comparative perspective, the life history of Oncorhynchus kisutch is an instructive example of a fast-growing, semelparous salmonid adapted to productive marine ecosystems. The species demonstrates a marked ontogenetic shift from a small, yolk-dependent alevin weighing 0.3137 grams [Wwb = 0.3137 grams] at emergence to a large, sexually mature adult exceeding 15,000 grams [Wwi = 15,000 grams]. The calculated wet weight at puberty of 10,800 grams [Wwp = 10,800 grams] highlights that a substantial proportion of somatic growth occurs before the final reproductive migration, and it underscores the critical need for adequate ocean feeding conditions. This developmental pattern, coupled with the extended 1,095-day (1,095 days) [tp = 1,095 days] period to puberty at 5 °C [T = 5 °C], contrasts with the life history of the sympatric pink salmon (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha), which returns to spawn after only a single year at sea. The total length of 108 cm [Li = 108 cm] also makes Coho one of the larger Pacific salmon species, rivaled only by Chinook salmon in maximum size.
